name: all-1
statement: The cued base and Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math differ in per-step math skill; the residual gap is a per-step knowledge deficit present from the first tokens of a solution, and the base's next-token distribution stays stable as its own generated solution grows (its loops at T 0.6 are an artifact of low-temperature sampling, and its unfinished answers at T 1.0 are searches on problems it does not know how to solve). Olmo-3.1's gain does not come from training truncated rollouts as negatives at 16k; it comes from the per-step reward signal it shares with 3.0, written as a concentrated change that shifts activations from the first token on and across all text, so the gap scales with problem knowledge, not with solution length or token budget.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base (with and without the opening cue) vs Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math and Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math (3.0), MATH-500 and the 328 harder problems, T 0.6-1.0, caps 4k-32k, weight interpolation base + a*(RL - base). It does not cover the plain (uncued) base's format failures, the Code pair, or pass@k ceilings.

explains.how: At a 31,744-token cap length stops limiting anyone, so these numbers measure per-step skill; the same paper's harder sets show RL ahead of the cued base by 5-12 points at that generous cap, a knowledge gap that no extra budget closes, and on MATH-500 the 3.0 model sits near the ceiling where the cue's format gain alone can match it.

explains.quote: not masking truncated sequences (they are trained as negatives)
explains.how: This change touches only the small share of rollouts that reach 16k; 3.0 and 3.1 share prompts, rewards and steps, and the bulk of the gradient in both comes from finished answers graded right or wrong, which teaches per-step correctness.

explains.quote: from RL's prefix 48 / 41 / 21; from its own prefix 23 / 16 / 38
explains.how: The own-prefix arm was cut just before the base's loop onset at T 0.6, so it inherits the repetition a low-temperature sampler had already set up; the right counts 41 vs 16 track the loop counts 21 vs 38, a sampling artifact, not a deficit in conditioning on its own text.

explains.quote: T1 cap hits exceed T2's by 15.2 points in Q4
explains.how: The longest quartile holds the hardest problems; a model that does not know the next step keeps searching until the cap, so excess cap hits mark missing knowledge, while the 10-20 point gap is present in every quartile as a per-step deficit predicts.

Both models spend the same budget (9,345 vs 9,316 tokens per problem); the base's cap hits are the problems it cannot solve, and RL itself is right on only 19 of those 77, so they are hard problems, not budget failures.

Loops appear at T 0.6 and vanish at T 1.0 (0 of 500 by rule A), which makes them a property of low-temperature sampling, not of the base's long context; at T 1.0 the base's own long text carries no repetition attractor.

explains.quote: diverge on math solutions, more with depth
explains.how: The divergence is as large on the base's own short answers as on RL's long ones and starts in layers 8-15, where per-step math is computed; it marks a different math policy at every step, not a repair that waits for long contexts.

Only 16 of the 65 RL-only items are unfinished and none of them loops, so the base did not degrade; it kept searching for a step it did not know, while the other 49 are finished answers with per-step errors.

explains.quote: the gain is more answers finishing under the cap
explains.how: That finishing gain came on a different model under a tight 4,096 cap and cost 11-20 points on GPQA and MBPP+; on Olmo at a 16k cap only 27 cued-base answers fail to finish, so finishing cannot carry a 53-answer gap.

conflicts.how: The gap grows from 11.2 points in the shortest quartile to 20.0 in the longest; the theory holds that this growth is difficulty, since the longest RL answers belong to the hardest problems, and the 11-point gap on the shortest problems is the per-step deficit itself.

conflicts.quote: finished with a wrong answer on 33
conflicts.how: Two thirds of the RL-only hard problems are finished wrong answers, as a per-step deficit predicts; the remaining 16 cap hits must be read as searches on unknown steps rather than as drift.
Misreads, slips and wrong methods (37 of 65) are per-step errors, the core of the theory; the 8 garbled final lines and 2 drifts are the residue it must still assign to per-step choices.

conflicts.quote: the top 4 % of positions carry 38.7 % of KL
conflicts.how: The theory predicts KL spread evenly over position; this readout ranks positions by size, not by place in the answer, so it does not test that claim, and RL's largest gaps on cap hits sit early (median relative position 0.19).

rival: The gap is a long-horizon self-conditioning deficit in the base, repaired by Olmo-3.1's training of truncated rollouts as negatives with a change that acts only deep inside long math contexts. Separation: the rival predicts KL(RL||base) per token on RL's own long answers rising with position, the gap closing or reversing at a 4k cap, and Olmo-3.0 RL (same steps, no truncation negatives) well below 3.1 at T 1.0. This theory predicts KL flat or falling over position, RL leading at every token cap, and 3.0 about as good as 3.1.

predictions.experiment: Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math (3.0 release), plain prompt, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, MATH-500 one sample
predictions.refuted_by: 3.0 scores 425 or less, far below 3.1's 463, or has more than twice 3.1's cap hits

predictions.experiment: Teacher-forced KL(RL||base) per token after the cue on RL's own T 1.0 MATH-500 answers longer than 8,000 tokens; ratio of mean KL in the last quarter of positions to the first quarter
Existing T 1.0 MATH-500 answers of the cued base (410) and RL (463) rescored with every answer truncated at 4,096 generated tokens (an unfinished answer counts wrong); RL minus cued base
predictions.refuted_by: RL ties or trails the cued base (difference 0 or below) at the 4,096 cap

predictions.experiment: Base continues at T 1.0 from the first 40 % of RL's right answer vs from the first 40 % of its own answer, on the base's 77 hard-328 cap-hit problems with the cue; difference in finish rate (no cap hit)
base + 0.5*(RL - base) with the cue, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, hard 328, grader v3, one sample; cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: cap hits fall below 50 while accuracy stays near the base's 164
